utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please sit down. Good afternoon to the interpreters. I hope they had a good rest and are ready to go on. I would like to greet the Defence counsel, and I shall ask Mr. Dubuisson to have the accused brought in. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So now I can greet both Prosecution and the Defence counsel. We are going to resume the proceedings. So we are having a witness; are there any protective measures with regard to this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, no protective measures was requested. We're dealing with Mr. Tolo Edvard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But Mr. Nobilo is going to tell us that exactly; isn't he?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, the name is Edvard Tolo who is the next Defence witness. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please stand up for a few moments. Please tell us your name, your date of birth, your place of birth. You're not a protected witness, so you can tell us your birth and what your occupation is, and only then will you read the oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Edvard Tolo. I was born on the 26th of June, 1960, in Hanover, and I live in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. The usher is going to show you the solemn declaration which you will please read out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. You agreed to come to testify as a Defence witness as asked by the Defence counsel of General Blaskic, who is accused for the International Criminal Tribunal. You're going to have questions put to you by the Defence to start with, then by the Prosecution, and the last stage by the Judges. Who is going to take the questions? Mr. Nobilo, you are going to; aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. Tolo, good afternoon. You said that you were born in Hanover, the Republic of Germany. Can you explain to the Trial Chamber, that is to say, your parents, which ethnicity do they belong to, although it wasn't important in Bosnia? Could you explain to the Court, please?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: I come from a mixed marriage. My father is a Croat, my mother is a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Which schools have you completed?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: I went to the military academy for higher military skills.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The military academy of the Yugoslav People's Army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Yes, of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Briefly, tell the Court, please, having completed your military academy training, I suppose you were in Belgrade for that; where did you take up active military service for the first time?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: I completed my schooling at the beginning of 1990, and my first service was in Postojna in the Republic of Slovenia. Then I was commander of a platoon and my first superior was Mr. Blaskic, as commander of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Having left the Yugoslav People's Army, where did you go then? Which organisation did you join?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: This was in 1992, and I became a member of the special police in Tuzla under the Lillies (phoen), and under the leadership of the BH army and the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: To make things simpler, in Tuzla the dominant power and authority was held by the Muslims Bosniaks; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: (No audible answer)

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you answer the question, please? Is it correct that you were in the units which was led by the government in Sarajevo, that is to say, the Bosniaks Muslims?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. While I was in Tuzla, from the beginning of 1992 to the latter half of 1992, I was in the special purpose police units, and the government in Sarajevo and the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina was in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You were wounded in those units; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Is it also correct that you returned to Vitez after that?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: In the first half of July I returned to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What do you do today?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Today I'm unemployed, and from time to time I'm a bus driver for a bus going from Vienna to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We're going to talk about where and when you first got to know first-class captain Tihomir Blaskic. Could you tell us the circumstances governing your first meeting?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: I met Mr. Blaskic for the first time as commander of the company. He had the rank of captain at the time. He was my immediate superior. In view of the fact that I had just come down from military academy with only theoretical knowledge, in addition to being my immediate superior, he was there to train me, that is, to train me in practical commanding matters and service duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us, please, when you say my immediate superior, what unit was this? Where was it located and what was its name?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: It was the unit in Postojna, part of the company of the 228th Brigade of the former JNA, and that was at the beginning of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Captain Blaskic, therefore, was your superior officer. Can you describe to us how you found him as an officer and a man, and how other people saw him? What was the impression he left on the units, on that particular unit of the Yugoslav People's Army? And I would like to ask you to slow down when answering, please. Try and speak as slowly as possible to enable our interpreters to interpret.

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: With his outer aspect and his attitude, his build and his behaviour, he was a man who was -- you could see he was an officer, whether he was wearing civilian clothes or a uniform, he was a true officer. He had all the characteristics and traits of a real commander. His conduct was such, the manner in which he issued his commands were such, and he set an example to people of what an officer should be. His relationship towards his subordinates was a correct one, but he did not allow for any intimacy, but kept to the ranks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Tolo, what was the system of assessment and appraisal in the JNA, the evaluation? Can you give us the levels of evaluation?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Unsatisfactory was the lowest level, satisfactory, very good and exceptional as the best and top level of grading, outstanding level.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Court what grading did Blaskic receive in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: While I was with him he had outstanding achievement, outstanding grades, the best grades possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In the environment in Slovenia, the JNA environment in Slovenia, was he considered to be the best officer with a good future ahead of him?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you remember anything as regards his advancement?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: While I was there he was promoted to the rank of captain first-class because of his merits and outstanding achievement in work, and that year very few officers were promoted. He is one of the rare individuals who were promoted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Through his work was he able to be promoted further but did not have the necessary years of service?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: As far as I know, through his work and the schooling he had, he had also passed the examination for major but was not able to move forward and be promoted because he didn't have enough years of service. So all he needed was an additional number of years of service to move from captain first-class to a higher rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In the JNA at that time, was it difficult to receive a promotion? Was it a very rigorous, rigid system through which the officers had to pass?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: There was promotion after a set number of years in the service, and if an unsatisfactory grade was received, then ranks would be deducted if there were any negative forms of conduct or anything else. The better the result the better the marks, the faster the promotion would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Court whether captain first-class Tihomir Blaskic had wielded authority, vis-a-vis his subordinates, and what his relationship was with them?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Well, in concrete terms towards his subordinates, first and foremost, he did wield authority by virtue of his uniform, and then also by virtue of his conduct, and he became an authority. He was an honest man, and towards his subordinate commanders, he never criticised anybody in front of the army for his work, but always did so -- he would take somebody aside and criticise them if he felt the need. He would never do this in front of anybody else, and thus built up his subordinates authority, as well. Towards the rank and file of the army, he was always objective in his conduct. I should like to mention that during our service in Slovenia, many soldiers were of the Albanian nationality, Albanian ethnicity, and I might add that he never had pretensions towards any nation, or for giving better marks to somebody with regard to his ethnicity or withholding those marks, whether they were from his area and from his ethnic group or not. For him, he had two groups of soldiers, a good soldier and a bad soldier. If somebody was bad, his behaviour towards him would correspond. If they were good, he would also react in the proper way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Now, towards bad soldiers, would he use measures of any kind, punishment, or would he reward good soldiers?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Yes, soldiers would be rewarded. They would get extra leave or anything else that the army provided for. Bad soldiers would be punished according to law, of course, and the rules and regulations of the former Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell the Court, please, you were, in practical terms, his neighbour from a neighbouring municipality, a Croat. You find yourselves in far off Slovenia; were you privileged by him in any way as compared to the others?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: No, I did not feel any preferential treatment towards me as being from his ethnic group, and my official marks were in the middle somewhere. I was satisfactory, no more, no less. He could have given me a better assessment, because in fact, the assessment he made of me did not influence his own final assessment or mark in any way. So it was immaterial whether he would give a higher or lower mark, but he was always objective and looked at things as they stood.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us, in addition to what you mentioned already, did he wield his authority in any other way? Did he use force? Did he hit the soldiers or did he use different methods to convince soldiers of what they are supposed to do, or junior officers?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Through our training and education, we also studied psychology. His methodology was psychological. He dealt with the soldiers' psychology. He made a soldier feel in a certain way. If he was guilty, then the soldier himself would feel guilty. He simply didn't want to punish soldiers for the sake of punishment. It was important for him to convince a soldier that he had done something wrong. In the army no one ever resorted to force in the former JNA, never. That would have had a negative impact on the overall assessment of a commander. Psychologically, by using words, he would mete out punishment, and that is how soldiers achieved better results, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What did he say about recording activities and orders? Tell the Court about this. This was back in 1990, I believe.

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: This is the first lesson I learned from him: All the orders that I give or receive, that I write down in a notebook, because that is a kind of document, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: With a properly organised army, can you agree with me that Blaskic enjoyed the reputation of the best officer, the best kind, one that was predestined to be a General?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Mr. Blaskic was an exemplary officer, an ideal. He was someone who was an example to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Now, we're going to move away from Slovenia where you served together. You were still in the JNA, and you came across Blaskic once again. This was in Tuzla. Could you just tell us a few sentences about the circumstances under which you met Colonel Blaskic then?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Mr. Blaskic was already a civilian. That day I was the officer on duty in the barracks and Mr. Blaskic was arrested, brought in by the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Yes, Yugoslav People's Army. He was a suspect, and he and another boy were taken in as suspects because they were found in a passenger vehicle. There was a bag of arm bands that they had in the car. Also, apparently Mr. Blaskic had not returned his uniform and his pistol, so they charged him with that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Military berets and arm bands that had the insignia of the Croatian army; right?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that was the case, but apparently all this belonged to the boy who was in the car with Mr. Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What about the pistol? Ultimately did they realise that he had rightly kept it?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: At the time when we were in Slovenia we had already paid for Zastivas (phoen) 357 and for new magnums, and we did not receive them while we were up there, and an agreement was reached that official pistols could be kept because we did not get the new pistols, and this would be a compensation for the pistols we had already paid for.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: After this second meeting, you saw HVO Colonel Blaskic in Vitez for the third time. Explain to the Court when this happened, under what circumstances and what you talked about.

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: It was my third time when I saw Mr. Blaskic in Vitez, in mid-July. This was the second day after I arrived from Tuzla. He was waiting for me in front of the house, in front of the entrance, with three more gentlemen who were with him and a soldier who was their escort, their security, and he was waiting in the yard. First we said hello to each other, and then he asked me whether I wanted to go to town and have a little talk with him, because we didn't want to irritate my parents, because it wasn't the usual thing for a group of soldiers to come to civilian houses, because this could only make the neighbours feel afraid, too. In the cafe, when we went downtown, he offered me to join his army. He offered me a commission. He offered me weapons, and finally he said that on the opposite side was the commander of the Serb forces in Vlasic, former Major Bosko Peulic. And it was a well-known fact that we had clashed in the former JNA, too. He said that, in a way, this way I could get my own way back to Peulic. However, the conversation that we had was not customary. It was not what I had been used to from him, because all the time these three other gentlemen whom I did not know kept interrupting him. They interrupted his sentences. They told him what to ask me. They gave him guidelines as to how he should speak. And I thought that he was the one who was in charge, and it seemed as if he was their subordinate, and this was in contrast to what I had been used to. That is to say, when senior people spoke juniors would keep quiet, and then they would ask for permission to speak, but that was not the situation then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Blaskic gave you an offer to join the army. Did you refuse that?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: At that point I did, because I was still wounded, because I could not take it physically at that point, and on the other hand, for many years I'd been separated from my father, and his wish was for me to spend more time with him, in a way, to make up for the time we had lost being together as father and son.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And did you also want to get some respite to see what the situation was altogether?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: After I arrived in Vitez I had already been on the frontline for a few months. In Vitez things were relatively peaceful, and I heard what individuals had to say at that point, and I was a bit offended too. Generally speaking, I was offended by their attitude towards the war. For them it was a game, and I had already seen what a war was really like, and I saw it on the ground, so I really needed a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You had graduated from the academy, and you already had some years of service in JNA troops, and you also spent some time actually fighting within Bosnia and Herzegovina with the Bosniak police, so could you tell the Court, as a civilian in Vitez and with all the knowledge you had had, everything I mentioned, your entire experience; what was your assessment? What was the kind of army that Blaskic commanded? What type of soldiers were there? What kind of units? Because, after all, you had a privileged position and you had a vantage point for viewing all of this.

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: As an observer from, the very outset, I could make a distinction between three different groups of soldiers there. The first group were the special purposes units, as independent soldiers. The first thing that was striking about them was that they had black attire. Should I describe it? So the first thing you could see was their black attire, their black uniforms. These were very young men as a rule, and they were Rambo copies from American movies, and they were well-equipped. They had good weapons, automatic rifles, good equipment, cartridge belts, soldier belts. All of it looked like from American movies, as I said. Also, they carried long rifles in town, which is unheard of, because it frightened civilians. Then they would even take these kind of weapons into cafes, and also then mixing weapons and alcohol, which gives rise to new danger. Then shooting, shooting in town without any reason whatsoever, carousing. Then many criminals joined these units and they were hiding behind these uniforms and behind what these units stood for. They would try to hide their own criminal records, their criminal past. Then also in the centre of every town there was some kind of special purpose unit. For example, in Vitez there was the Vitezovi, and most of them were locals from Vitez. They were the strongest, and they dominated Vitez. All of them were very young men, tough guys, strong. On the other hand, they were inexperienced. They had the town under their control, particularly cafes and restaurants, and their command was even in a Cafe.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, how could we characterise these young men, as former street gangs?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, was their total loyalty to their commander Darko Kraljevic? Could anybody replace Darko Kraljevic and put someone else in command?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: No. Darko Kraljevic, the late Darko Kraljevic, was God in their eyes. Whatever he said was sacred. That was the gospel. No one dared oppose him and they all appreciated him very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that every such territory had this kind of unit which was a local unit and held this territory under their control. In Vitez it was the Vitezovi. What about Nova Bila? Who was in charge there?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Zuti and Krupce. They also had a Special Purposes Unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I imagine you were not familiar with the situation in other towns, but tell us, was there some kind of solidarity between these street gangs, or let us call them special purposes units? Were there any clashes between them?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: There was an unwritten agreement that one would not interfere in the turf of the other. That is to say, the Vitezovi would not go to Nova Bila and the other way around. Zuti does not go to Vitez. So they did not interfere in each other's affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: There is an exception?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When Tuka, the commander of one such unit, and Zuti the commander of another such unit --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me. I would ask if there's an exception, that counsel ask what the exception is as opposed to explaining what the exception is ahead of time. It's purely a matter of form.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: There was a principle that such special purposes units do not clash between themselves, but there was only one exceptional event, and can you explain to the Court which was this exceptional event?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: There were the Mujna under the command of the late Tuka. These Mujna, Thunders -- or, rather, the commander of Mujna and Zuti clashed, and the late Tuka, on one occasion, shot at Zuti, wounded him, and he ended up in hospital, and finally in a wheelchair too. In retaliation, the bodyguards, the soldiers, whatever you want to call them, of Zuti, took revenge of Tuka, and killed him in town, far away from the frontline. This was actually in revenge terms of what he did to Zuti.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In your opinion, looking at it from the sides, do you think that Blaskic could have commanded Darko Kraljevic, Zuti and similar individuals as a commander vis-a-vis his subordinates?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Under conditions of these kind, not at all. At no events.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And if he wanted to use the Vitezovi, what would Blaskic have to do?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Blaskic would have to reach an agreement about this and find a compromise solution, and convince the unit and Darko to send a certain number of soldiers to do something or to be included into anything of this kind. So Darko was the ultimate person making the decision. Everything else was on the basis of decision making.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You have now described briefly the special purpose units. What was the other group, recognisable group, of military units in the area of Vitez municipality?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Well, there was a village -- every village had one unit, because the locals of a village would rally round in defence of their village and so make up a unit. Within these units they would elect their representative. As opposed to the first instance, they were much -- of much less weaponry, were not as well-equipped, and they commented the orders, whereas they did not have a commander whom they followed blindly, which was as in the case of the first group. If they appointed a commander, they would replace him and comment his decisions, comment his orders. It was the will of the locals as a whole. So if somebody made a decision that didn't agree to the locals, they would raise up their voices and criticise the decision made, and they would organise sort of village watches to begin with, and set up defence barricades in their own villages. So within this circle they did not have a barracks. Everybody went home to their own houses, and they would take the weapons home with them to their house overnight. As a military formation, they were not able to function properly because they were fragmented, dispersed, and nobody could actually rally the forces and command them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You mean to say that control was made more difficult. Why?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Well, if there is one commander then he cannot be in all houses at the same time. He hasn't got an insight into what is going on, so he could have several individuals going around with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And where were the soldiers usually to be found?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: The soldiers were in their own homes, in their own houses. If they took part in the village watch, they would spend a couple of hours every evening together and then go home, because everything took place within the confines of a village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What about uniforms and rifles? Where did they keep them?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: They kept them with them. First of all, they were hunting rifles, repetition rifles and a little more modern weaponry but not much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So in addition to the units which represented the village, or the village which represented a unit in itself, and in addition to the special purpose units, which was the third group that was recognisable and could be distinguished in the Vitez area?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: It was the Vitez battalion with Mr. Cerkez and Mr. Bertovic. In fact, it was, as I was able to understand at the time, an active composition of -- with active commanders. Later on, when they were mobilised, when this reserve unit was mobilised, they were placed under their command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What about the reserve formations of the Vitez Brigade? That was the village units; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you tell me the characteristics of the Vitez battalion, who commanded them and whether the commanders were appointed democratically or was it established in a different way altogether?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: The Vitez brigade could be placed as the basis of a new -- could form the basis of a new army, because little by little, we had the superiority/subordination relationship established. Mario Cerkez was the main commander, and his subordinates were well-known and they had to follow orders from him, but as a military formation, they did not have enough men to be able to perform all the tasks and duties that a unit of that kind should have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell the Trial Chamber, please, you graduated from the military academy. You have had the benefit of the JNA practical training. What you learned at the academy and army, was all this knowledge applicable to the situation that prevailed and the army that existed as it did in Vitez at that time, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: No, not under such conditions, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber, please, whether the civilian police and the Military Police could allow itself to arrest Zuti, one of the Zuti men, or somebody else?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: No. There was too great a fear of the same. So not even the Military Police or the civilian police. They avoid all contacts, all official contacts, with members of this unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: After some time had elapsed, you, nonetheless, took part in the military structures of the HVO. Could you explain to us the components of this and what your duties were?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: From October 1993, Mr. Blaskic -- I received orders from Mr. Blaskic to report to him, and he deployed me to Nova Bila, to the barracks, and the primary school there, which was turned into a barracks. The idea was, and I had received orders along those lines, for me to take over the soldiers there as an instructor, to train the soldiers in dealing with weapons and handling weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us, please, was it a young army? Was it made up of young men who had never had any military experience?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: They were young soldiers, 18 years of age, had become adolescents, but had not done their military training.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Before those young soldiers, were training sessions organised in Vitez, as you, in fact, organised in the autumn of 1993?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: The training centre, such as the one existed in Nova Bila, did not exist, only along the frontlines where there was a crash course as to how to load your rifle and how to shoot your rifle, but that was very sparse.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell the Court, please, how many young men went to this primary school in Nova Bila?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: There were about 100 of them, perhaps a little less.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Would you describe to us now, please, what you actually did? What did the training consist of, and who drew up a plan and programme for the training?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Well when I went to Nova Bila, I had already heard that these men had been functioning for a month to two months before my arrival. They were under the command of Mr. Vukovic, and they worked according to Mr. Vukovic's programme. It was my task to train them in dealing with and handling rifles and weapons. I tested a few of the young men to see what knowledge they had already gained, but I saw that in practical terms they knew nothing, and I suggested to Mr. Vukovic that we start from the beginning, from zero, and then I drew up a plan and programme of training myself, which I was to implement. I used the model of the former JNA, the number of hours of training for each particular category of weapon, and Mr. Vukovic accepted this training programme. So we started from scratch.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Apart from rifles, did you have any other aids? Did you have a military training polygon?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Well, the school was turned into a barracks very rapidly. There were some classrooms. We threw out the desks from other classrooms to make room for beds where the men could sleep. We had a blackboard and chalk, and, in fact, we had weaponry which were no longer very effective and efficient on the frontline. We had a small meadow behind the school building to train in, so the training programme that I was in charge of was, in fact, more or less theoretical, because we did not have the necessary equipment and means to actually go into practical training.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell the Court, please, whether you were able to have any tactical training, and if so, what group of people did you do this training with?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: As we had very restricted space and the terrain was such that I had a group of, say, ten soldiers to train, and even there we would collide with one another or we would lose the soldiers. They would become scattered around the countryside. So we weren't able to go very far because we weren't that far from the frontlines.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Before you took over this purely military function and duty, Blaskic had ordered you to take part in a project which was to have held in these -- reigned in the special purposes unit. Could you tell us what that was all about?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Sometime in August, Mr. Blaskic told me to go to Prahulja and to contact a Colonel there. I don't remember his name. He did not give me any details, but when I got there this commander told me that there was an idea to form a (inaudible) unit which -- intervention unit to intervene on occasion, and I was one of the commanders of the platoon. When I was told that these special purpose units were to form this composition, were to form the company, I found this ludicrous, because it was impossible to put them altogether and to function in this way. So I left the commander my telephone number, and if he ever succeeded in doing so I told him to call me, but I did not really believe in the possibility of forming a unit of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did he ever telephone?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: No, he never called me. So that means that he never succeeded in pulling this off.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You personally found yourself in a very delicate situation. You could not have -- betray your father or mother. You were from a mixed marriage and you had two ethnic groups in your parents. Could you tell us whether Blaskic discussed the situation with you ever?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me. With all due respect, I mean -- certainly the comments of counsel are not evidence, and I just would -- I would ask, Mr. President and Your Honours, if counsel would ask the questions and let the witness answer the question without giving a preface to the question concerning what this individual -- this man's position was. Just let the man speak for himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, you all do so, whether from the Prosecution, from the Defence, but try and limit your comments as much as you can. Do endeavour to meet the Prosecution's concerns, Mr. Nobilo, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very simply, did Blaskic ever show any interest in your personal situation and your attitude towards the conflict between the Muslim and Croat ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: On one occasion he told (sic) me to -- to headquarters and then we finally had this private conversation. He of all, asked me firstly, naturally, about my parents' health, how the folks at home were, and then he asked me about my own views, because he knew I was from a mixed marriage. I told him, "We are defending ourselves here, and if my own father were to shoot at me, I would answer with fire."

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. President. We have thus conclude our questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Tolo. My name is Greg Kehoe from the Office of the Prosecutor. My two colleagues are Mr. Harmon, and to the far right is Mr. Cayley. Welcome. Mr. Tolo, were you in the HVO when you returned to Vitez in July of 1992? Did you join it?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Not straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When did you join the HVO?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: A few months later my father bought me a Combi van and I drove between Vitez and Travnik and there was work duty. When soldiers were supposed to be taken to Slatkevode, to the frontline against the Serbs, but this was within my own private activities, within my own private business, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, my question for you, Mr. Tolo, is when did you join the HVO? Give me a date.

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: I don't understand. You mean as a soldier or as an officer?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Any way. Just part of the HVO. Soldier, officer, you know, anything.

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: As a soldier, this was the end of 1991. As a soldier, driver, who would drive to Slatkevode every now and then, this was my first active contribution to the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Are you talking about the end of 1992? I think you might have misspoke on the transcript, if I might be mistaken, counsel. Are you saying that you joined the HVO at the end of 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Until '94, when I was finally demobilised. This is to say, after the conflict between the Croats and the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So it would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me. It is '91 or '92, finally?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is actually 1991, Judge. I'll have a document for him. The witness actually got into the HVO in September of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me. It's in 1992, Judge. The transcript had 1991, and I believe we corrected it. It is in 1992. I made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: September, was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm going to ask him about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, if I can show the witness a document, this is only in B/C/S. Mr. Usher?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit 549.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Unfortunately, Mr. President, and Counsel, this is only in the B/C/S language; but on that page that is a list of individuals in the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolo, your are on that page, are you not? You can see your birth date being the 22nd of June, 1970?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I don't know where you are. I didn't quite grasp what you are doing. Could you give us the page again, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The second page of the document, Mr. President, we have the names down, one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, ninth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That's right. Nine, Tolo Edvard. Thank you very much, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's you, is it not, Mr. Tolo?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Yes, except that this is the citizen's registration code next to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It does reflect you were in the HVO from 1 September, 1992 to 1 July of 1994; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So as of the 1st of September, 1992, sir, you were in the HVO wearing a uniform that had the HVO logo on the sleeve; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: That is not correct, because there weren't enough uniforms, so I had some of my former JNA clothes. At that time I was working as a driver with the defence department.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were you considered a soldier within the HVO, sir, working for the defence department driving soldiers around?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So did you tell either Mr. Nobilo or any of the Defence counsel that you declined to join the HVO military? Did you ever tell them that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Could we have a time frame?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm reading your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Ask him about the spring of 1992, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: "After the witness left the JNA he returned to the Vitez municipality. He declined to join the HVO military and instead undertook various alternate forms of service, including driving HVO soldiers from place to place." So when were you driving soldiers from place to place, you were a member of the HVO military; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Counsel is asking several questions here. If he wants to know, in the spring of 1992, if the witness was asked to become active duty in the HVO, and if the witness declined, why don't he pose that question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Wait a minute. For the time being, Mr. Hayman, would you mind letting Mr. Kehoe ask the questions? The witness will answer. You are not the witness, Mr. Hayman. For the time being everything is very clear. Mr. Tolo, you understand that the Prosecution was trying to ascertain, as is its right, what time it was when you joined, when it was that you joined the HVO. We have got an official document, and according to this document you were an HVO member by September '92. I think we should leave it at that for the time being. Please specify the dates, Mr. Kehoe, so as to reassure Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You came back to the Vitez municipality in July of 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that is in the summer of 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Yes, it was summertime. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And summer follows spring; don't it?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Yes, naturally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So after you got back to Vitez in the summer of 1992, by September of 1992, you were a member, a soldier in the HVO; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Wait a minute, Mr. Kehoe. Please be specific. I know summer follows spring, but could you be more specific? We're talking about the 1st of September. Is that the date when the witness joined the HVO? And he came back to Vitez a few weeks earlier; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That would appear to be what the records reflect and what the witness now reflects. My only problem, of course, is the summary that was provided to us that says "After the witness left the JNA he returned to the Vitez municipality." New sentence, "He declined to join the HVO military and instead undertook various alternate forms of service, including driving HVO soldiers from place to place."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, that is the summary provided by Mr. Nobilo, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, my colleague did this, but never mind. It would be fair, though, to ask the witness, because my colleague is asserting various things and don't leave any time for the witness to put a question, he hasn't asked him a thing yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, I'll have you notice that you were the ones to interrupt, Mr. Kehoe, rather than the opposite. Ask your questions, Mr. Kehoe, and you will have your time again in due time for the Defence. You have the floor, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The bottom line Mr. Tolo, is that by 1 September 1992, you were a soldier in the HVO; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness's microphone is not on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The witness's microphone is not on. He's not supposed to be putting it on. Maybe you turned it off by mistake, Mr. Tolo.

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: From the 1st of September, that's what it says, I was an HVO soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay, and what rank did you hold when you were an HVO soldier?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: At that time nobody paid much attention to rank, so I functioned as a soldier, but I had retained the rank I had in the former JNA, but it had not been translated into a new rank with the Croatian Defence Council, yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So were you a lieutenant in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, the rank that you had in the JNA was a lieutenant; was it not?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: According to the new translation I was a lieutenant in the former JNA, but then I turned into a warrant officer second class in the HVO. But nobody really paid much attention to it at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So in the HVO you would have been called possibly a warrant officer second class; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Why do you say second class? I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, if it's just warrant officer, period, I stand corrected, because I thought that's what the translation said.

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: I'm a noncommissioned officer in translation, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now as a noncommissioned officer, what were your duties and responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: I was a soldier and a driver, and nobody made me do anything else. I wasn't supposed to give or take orders. So I was simply supposed to drive during my tour of duty, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you work in the Hotel Vitez as part of the command with Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: What period are you asking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: From when you took -- from 1992, or any time, did you work in the Hotel Vitez? If you did, tell us when it started.

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: I was sent from October 1993 to the Nova Bila barracks. I was sent by headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now prior to October of 1993, were you part of the Hotel Vitez command structure at all?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: No. My immediate superior was Mr. Zibonjic (phoen) of the defence department until the conflict with the Muslims broke out. As soon as the conflict broke out between the Muslims and the Croats, as a soldier/driver, I was given to the Vitez Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you were not part of the Hotel Vitez command structure at all, or at least not before October of 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you see the written orders that Colonel Blaskic issued to the Vitezovi?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: The Vitezovi? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you see the written orders that were written by Colonel Blaskic to the Zuti special purpose unit?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you a document, and this is a Defence document, Defence Exhibit 250. Now before we move to that document, you said you never saw any written orders issued by Blaskic to the Vitezovi. Were you part of discussions between Blaskic and Darko Kraljevic, where Blaskic discussed with Darko Kraljevic what to do?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: I was never present on such an occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay, so you never saw any orders and you were never present on any occasion where Blaskic discussed with Darko Kraljevic what to do. Let me turn your attention to Exhibit 250, and let us turn our attention to -- and bear with me a second. I know the page in the English version and I will just see if I can find it in the B/C/S version. Maybe you can help us out, Mr. Tolo. Look for the first date that starts the 16th of April, 1993. Did you find that, sir? It pretty much goes in chronological order, if you can move down the pages quickly. I think it's on page 4 of the B/C/S version, about halfway down, it says "Dana, 16.04, 1993;" do you see that?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Yes, I see it here, the 16th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let me tell you, Mr. Tolo, this is a Defence exhibit that was introduced and it is a report by the Vitezovi back to the defence department in Mostar. Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you the 16th of April, 1993. It notes that a battle team of 18 soldiers cleared the area of the gas station Kalenn, Rakita, Novaci, and it notes that on that occasion several Vitezovi were wounded and Ivan Zuljevic was killed. Who gave the order for those 18 soldiers to clear that gas station? You know where that gas station is don't you?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: I'm familiar with the area, but I don't know who could have issued this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's go down to the next line, next sequence, next paragraph. It says after that, "The PPN Vitezovi was engaged in the forming of the frontline against the Muslims from Vitez to Busovaca;" do you see that in the statement?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: I don't understand. I mean, I see it, but I don't see what your question is. I don't understand what your question is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Here is my question: Who gave the order to deploy the Vitezovi to the frontline against the Muslims from Vitez to Busovaca? Who gave them that order?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: I don't know, because I did not have any insight into these orders or I didn't know what the soldiers were doing, and I don't know who could have issued these orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Look at the rest of these, sir. When we go down that page the fact of the matter is, on all these orders, such as the 6 soldiers on the 18th of April, going to Crkva Vitez, and the 18th of April going to Stari Vitez, and the 19th of April going to Gornja Veceriska; you have no idea who gave the orders to deploy those Vitezovi to those areas, is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: The only person who could have commanded the Vitezovi was Mr. Darko Kraljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you know if Blaskic gave them that order?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolo, do you have any facts to support your contention that the Vitezovi -- let me withdraw that. Do you know of an instance when the Vitezovi refused an order of Colonel Blaskic, and if you do know that, tell the Judges.

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: I cannot give a single example. I don't know who else could have ordered the Vitezovi but Darko Kraljevic. Nobody else. It is quite obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, it is true, is it not, Mr. Tolo, that the Vitezovi were under the operational command of Colonel Blaskic while they were in the Central Bosnian Operative Zone? Isn't that true? Or do you not know that?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: No, no, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you don't even know whether or not they were under the operational command of Blaskic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you a couple of orders, if I may, -- excuse me, I'm sorry, 456/37, if I may, at the outset. That's a Prosecution exhibit. There is a French version, Mr. President, as well as a B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We're going to have a break at 3.30, because this is going to be a long afternoon, so we will have a break at 3.30; or do you have a lot of questions to put to this witness? We're going to have two breaks during this afternoon, a short one to start with, and I wouldn't like to cut off at a time where it might be difficult for you. What do you think?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I have a couple more questions, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So we may as well stop now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We can stop now, Mr. President, or we can finish this one document, or I can go to 3.30, or whatever Your Honour wants to do. If I can finish this document and move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine. Okay, you finish this document and then we will have a short break. Thank you very much. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tolo, this is a document that has been received in evidence dated the 19th of June, 1993; isn't that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: I can hardly see the date here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, certainly June of 1993; can you see that?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: I can see June, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We'll work off June of 1993, a period of time you were in the HVO. This particular command is issued by Blaskic to all independent units under the command of the HVO 3rd Operative Zone commander. And in that, in those independent units under the command of the 3rd Operative Zone commander, that is Colonel Blaskic, is the Vitezovi and also Zuti; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: It says here that in all brigades and independent units, but who exactly commanded them, that I don't know. But since we were surrounded, I imagine that it had to be under the command of the command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Tolo, I will read you the English version that was signed by Colonel Blaskic. And in this English version he relates, he gives this distribution of this order to all the independent units under the command of the HVO 3rd Operative Zone commander, and to MTD, the 4th LTRD, the 4th Military Police Battalion, the Vitezovi, Tvrtko 2 and Zuti. Do you have any knowledge of these units being under the command of Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So Mr. Tolo, you have no facts about orders issued by Blaskic, conversations between Darko Kraljevic and Blaskic, or whether or not the Vitezovi or these other units were under Blaskic's operational control; do you? You have no knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: I did not see a single order, and I didn't see that they were meeting with one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My last point is: You have no knowledge about what the relationship was between Vitezovi and Blaskic; do you?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: I know about the relationship between Blaskic and Vitezovi. I know there was some problems with regard to giving any kind of orders to Mr. Darko Kraljevic. It was very difficult to issue orders to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Give the Court one order Blaskic gave to Darko Kraljevic that you know about that Darko Kraljevic and the Vitezovi refused to obey. Give us one.

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: I am not aware of Mr. Blaskic having issued any order to the Vitezovi.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We can take a break right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine. This will be a 15-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please have the accused brought in. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please excuse us for the short delay. Breaks are not breaks necessarily for Judges. As soon as we get to the Chambers we're snowed under, a lot of requests, so we have to deal with them, but you have the floor, Mr. Kehoe, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you said that the independent units such as the Vitezovi and the Zuti were filled with criminals. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that. I mentioned the Vitezovi. Zuti I only know from hearsay, the stories told by the soldiers that I drove when passing through Bila.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But to your knowledge, you said the Vitezovi was filled with criminals; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: There were several of them who damaged the reputation of the Vitezovi.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did everybody know that?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Not everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did Blaskic know that?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: I don't know whether he did or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You don't know whether Blaskic knew or didn't know that these members of the Vitezovi had some criminal actions in their past; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: General Blaskic moved around in commanders' circles, so he didn't have any close contacts with the soldiers -- or contacts at all with the soldiers. Hierarchically, we go down to the soldiers via their commanders, so he would know what his subordinates would inform him of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let's speak about Blaskic and his subordinates. You have offered us some opinions during your testimony on direct. Were you present when Blaskic had meetings with Mario Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: No, not as a soldier/driver. I could not have been present at a meeting of that kind, but I know that Mario Cerkez went to him frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And how did Dusko Grubicic, the commander of the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade. Do you know Mr. Grubicic?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: I don't know him, no. Perhaps I met him but I don't know him by name. I don't know who that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How about meetings with Blaskic and his other brigade commanders. Did you sit in on those meetings?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: I've already said I was in the role of a soldier/driver, so I could not have been present at meetings of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you don't know anything about Blaskic's command as it related to the brigade commanders and as it related to other units under his command, do you, because you were just a driver and a soldier?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: I only know what I was told by the soldiers who were with me, and they very often distorted the picture of Blaskic. Blaskic was a foreigner down there in those parts, and they thought, "Why do we need somebody from outside to come and impose his power and authority over us?" So they would make jokes and fun of Blaskic, and they would say, "He's asked Darko to do something once again," and sort of make a joke of it, and said, "Darko promised to do something," but these were stories told by the soldiers, and the Vitezovi would boast about their commander and that Blaskic had to ask their commander for things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Tolo, you said, during your direct-examination, that the Military Police and the civilian police wouldn't arrest Zuti; is that right? Or his soldiers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Well, there was fear. There was fear of conduct of this kind. A lot of people were afraid of the repercussions and ensuing reactions after something like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, as a soldier within the HVO, do you know that Blaskic disciplined soldiers within the Zuti Special Purposes Unit?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: I don't know. Once again, I only know the circle around Vitez. We were bent on the Defence of Vitez, whereas the Zuti were in Nova Bila.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, the military disciplinary court was in Vitez; wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: I don't understand what kind of court you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let's take a look at Defence Exhibit 237 and 239. These are Defence exhibits admitted during the Defence case through the testimony of Brigadier Slavko Marin. D237 and D238 (sic). Mr. Usher, you can show the witness both of those exhibits at the same time, both 237 and 239. Mr. Tolo, did you ever see these documents before?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: I'm seeing them for the first time. This is the first time that I've seen this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tolo, in those documents, Blaskic and the HVO command in Vitez are disciplining Zuti -- members of the Zuti Special Purposes Unit for refusing to follow orders; isn't that right? Both of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, can we leave the witness some time to acquaint himself with the documents, because he says that he hasn't had occasion to see them? So can we give him time to read the title, the date and so forth?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I certainly apologise, Mr. Tolo. I don't mean to rush you through those documents in any way. If you need more time to study those documents, please take it. I apologise, counsel, and to the bench. I didn't mean to rush the witness through the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolo, let us know when you've had a chance to acquaint yourself with those documents.

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Yes, you can ask me your question now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Tolo, the fact is that in both of those orders -- I'm sorry. If we can just wait one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolo, the fact is that in both of those orders, the HVO is disciplining, issuing 30 days in gaol, to two members of the Zuti Special Purposes Unit who refused to follow orders, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, but I should like to mention that this is a period in which Mr. Blaskic had already taken over control of certain units. For example, starting with me myself, orders of October, I was doing things with my school, whereas of October 1993, for example, officers from the reserve force of the former JNA that had certain military knowledge were appointed to commanding posts, and some sort of organisation was established and control was being set up, so something could be done in that direction at that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolo, did you tell us that during direct-examination?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Could you repeat your question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you tell us what you just said concerning Blaskic setting up structures within Central Bosnia, did you tell us that during your direct-examination upon questions with Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: That as of October I was performing the function that I was? I'm not quite clear. What do you mean exactly? What do you want me to tell you? Because as of October -- I was appointed to the post in October and the structure was changing, the structure of command. More and more power and authority was being won over in the military structures. Prospects were being opened up for command going down to the subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, sir, you haven't -- you had not seen those documents before I showed them to you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: That's correct, I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you know of other members of the Zuti Special Purposes Unit who were disciplined?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: I remember an event that took place at the beginning the year, where the civilian police arrested the members of Zuti, and Mr. Zuti, with his team, came to free him, and he took control of the entire police station. When he found that the detainee was not at the police station but was in prison, they freed him and marched through the town and demonstrated their power and authority, and showed signs that he was the ruling power and that this was not to be repeated. That is a story about the Zuti and the rest. This took place at the beginning of 1993, and the picture then was quite different.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What is the date of those orders where these two individuals are disciplined?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: The 6th of November, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What date is the other one, the one on your right hand -- the one by your right hand? Turn it over.

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: The order was issued on the 26th of November and made known on the 29th of November, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: The second one, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolo, was anybody -- was Zuti or any member of Zuti disciplined for the event that you just talked about? The event of breaking that person out of prison, was anybody disciplined for that?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: I'm not aware of it. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You were in the HVO from 1992 -- September of 1992. These orders are in November. Let's take you to a starting point. You don't know anybody in the Vitezovi being disciplined for that outrageous act in the prison in November, December, January of 1994, through the time you left in July of 1994 and thereafter; is that right? I'm sorry, in the Zuti. If I said "Vitezovi", I meant "Zuti." Zuti or nobody else was disciplined for that act of breaking a member of the Zuti Special Purposes Unit out of gaol; were they?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: I haven't got any knowledge of that, so I can't tell you anything in any detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's move on, sir. Now, with regard to that particular event, did the Military Police have the power to stop the Vitezovi from breaking that person out of gaol -- excuse me, Zuti, I apologise, Zuti from breaking that person out of gaol?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Whether they had an order to do this I don't know, but I know that nobody dared stand up to them at that time, starting with the commander, right down to the ordinary rank-and-file soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let me show you an exhibit, and I'll show you again Defence Exhibit 213. This is an order -- or a report by Pasko Ljubicic concerning the event that you discussed. Take a look at this report. It deals with Zuti breaking Ferdo Gazibaric out of the Kaonik Prison. I ask you to turn to the last page of the document where Pasko Ljubicic, the commander of the 4th Military Police battalion notes as follows: "I received, on time, the information about the intentions of this group to free Gazibaric by means of firearms, and at the same time I warned about what would happen, so that there were many possibilities to organise the Military Police units and prevent this group on time in their intentions." So Mr. Tolo, from this Defence exhibit, the commander of the 4th Military Police Battalion himself said that he could have stopped Zuti and his men from completing this act. Have you seen that document before you came here today?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: No, I haven't seen that document before. But according to this report, he pushes the responsibility onto somebody else. He saw all this, put it on paper and passed it on to somebody else to protect himself from doing so. It doesn't say he would undertake this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolo, did it occur to you that Colonel Blaskic did not want to arrest Zuti and his men? Did that occur to you?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: It's possible, but I doubt it, because this would be negative for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, the fact of the matter is that in the entire time you were in Central Bosnia, Zuti nor any of his men were prosecuted or charged in any court for this outrageous conduct at Kaonik camp; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: I was not informed of whether anybody was prosecuted. I didn't hear of anything like that happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, the second prong of your discussion about the problems within Central Bosnia focused in villages and villagers. Do you recall that second prong in your direct examination by Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: You mean when I described the village, a village unit as being a unit?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you said that if someone, if the decision was made and someone in the village didn't like the decision, they would protest the decision; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Yes, and I have examples of this. For example, when I took the people to Slatkevode, we knew a village should give, let's say, five soldiers, and there would be a lot of argument, "Why do I have to go? Why doesn't he go?" So there were quarrels going on before they entered the vehicle. Then once we would start off for the place, there would be the same kind of situation once again, and he would go back home and say, "Why me, why aren't the soldiers? Their weapons weren't checked, the soldiers weren't examined" and so on. And when we returned from the frontlines on one occasion when there were problems on the Muslim side of Kalinska (phoen) and we weren't able to pass through, and they shouted that we should go home, "I have had an enough of the frontline, I'm hungry, I'm dirty, I want to go home" and the other half would be waiting for a government representative to turn up, and then together with the military police or the civilian police would enable safe passage and so on. So there was a lot of shouting, arguments, and the commanders couldn't do anything much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But the soldiers went; didn't they?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Very often what happened was that the soldiers appointed did not go but others would go, because they would decide this matter amongst themselves, and they would say, "Listen, you go now and I will go next time."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you went there to pick up five soldiers and you picked up five soldiers; right?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Five soldiers from one village, then perhaps ten soldiers from another, until I had filled up my vehicle, and then we would go in column towards Slatkevode.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolo, you were in the JNA and you know that the JNA defence of the former Yugoslavia was based on the Territorial Defence system; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Yes, but there was a skeleton in terms of the active corps of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when the HVO was set up and they had these individual village units, they were following the format that had been set up by the JNA; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: In many cases everything that resembled the JNA, or the Serbian part as such, they simply rejected it out of hatred. They said this was the occupier's way of thinking, et cetera, et cetera. So many rules, many formations that existed in the former army were simply skipped. They said all of that was pro-communist, pro-Yugoslav, and a lot of that was simply rejected, a lot of these previous principles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, allow me to tell you that the examination-in-chief lasted 45 minutes. You're going over that line now, so think of it so it remains within the ratio.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will move as quickly as I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolo, the HVO, like the JNA, was based on the Territorial Defence system; wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: I cannot say exactly about these formations, because from what I could see, the HVO was formed for the purpose of accelerated defence from aggression. At first there was no special kind of defence. People bought weapons on their own. They took away weapons on their own, and then village by village they tried to get weapons, and also the special purpose units were set up. But there was no traditional Territorial Defence system like with the warehouses that existed, et cetera. It was not exactly according to the picture that existed in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's talk a little bit about training, and we will go through this very briefly. You said you started training HVO soldiers in October of 1993. You do know that there was training of HVO soldiers going on in Central Bosnia and elsewhere in Herceg-Bosna prior to that; don't you?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: While I was there I was not aware of any other barracks except the one in Draga, but most of that was warehouses too, and I cannot speak about Herzegovina because I wasn't there. So I am not aware of any kind of training of soldiers taking place anywhere, before the barracks in Nova Bila, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Take a look at Prosecution Exhibit 456/104, 105, 106, 107 and 108. Those exhibits, Mr. Tolo, are a series of training orders signed by Colonel Blaskic between July of '92 and March of 1993. Now, that was a time period you were in Vitez; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: I cannot see the dates, exactly. During this period of time I was in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you know that from July of 1992 through at least March of 1993 and thereafter, Blaskic issued a series of orders to conduct training of HVO troops?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: I am not aware of him issuing such orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you a photograph, 433/8. Mr. Tolo, take a look at this on the ELMO. This is a photograph that was received in evidence by former Captain Lee Whitworth of the Prince of Wales own regiment of Yorkshire in the summer of 1993 where he testified that HVO troops were training in the Vitez area. This was a photograph that he took. Are you aware of the training taking place in the summer of 1993?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: I am not aware of that. Seems quite strange to me, because as far as I can see, these are former JNA uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's fine, sir. Now, sir, let us turn to another subject. You said during the JNA time that Blaskic was a very excellent officer who knew the rules and was destined to be a general; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I think you said he was the best officer in Slovenia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: He was a strong man, was he not?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: In what sense do you mean that? As a strong personality, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: He was a strong personality, which made him an excellent officer; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Not only that, but his knowledge, too. And the way he built up authority, he was a great psychologist, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And he knew the rules, and how to apply those rules in order to discipline his troops; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And all of that put together, his strength as an officer, his use of psychology, his knowledge of the rules, and his fairness in dealing with soldiers made him, in your view, an outstanding officer; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: All of that together, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And it was no surprise to you that in the summer of 1994, Blaskic became Chief of Staff of the HVO; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the year?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, it was the summer of 1994, he became Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when he became commander. You're meaning 1994? This was after the war. You mean after the war? For the merits and for his contribution, yes, certainly he deserved it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
