utterances.text: Now, you mentioned during your direct examination an individual who you served under in Slovenia by the name of Bosko Peulic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Bosko what?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Bosko Peulic.

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Did I mention my superior, Major Bosko Peulic, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Peulic, pardon my pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Bosko Peulic was in the command of the 228th Brigade, basically the right-hand of the commander of the brigade. Very often he came for controls, and very often he created problems for me. He discredited me in front of the other soldiers as I was teaching them, training them. I mean, I was a very young officer and I was inexperienced, and I certainly made many mistakes, but to tell me directly and in front of all the soldiers, that's not the way he was supposed to do it. He built his authority by trampling upon other people's authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And in Slovenia, he was Blaskic's immediate commander; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: He was above Blaskic. He was in the command of the brigade. He was deputy commander in the brigade, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And where was he during the fighting when you were in Vitez in July of 1992, and he was part of the Bosnian Serb army; where was he serving?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: He was in a brigade which was in Banja Luka, and very often he would go out to Vlasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The Vlasic feature, which is the mountain overlooking the Lasva Valley area?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Above the Lasva River Valley; that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you a document, Prosecution 528, if I may, Mr. Dubuisson. Take a look at that document, Mr. Tolo, and I ask you to look at that signature page. This is a letter concerning negotiations with Ustashe, being the Bosnian Serbs, and it is signed by the commander, Bosko Peulic. Do you see that signature?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: I see the signature of Mr. Peulic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's the same man you served under and Blaskic served under in Slovenia; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Yes, by his name and surname, but he just got a different rank afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tolo, my last subject, and just a couple of questions about this. You said you were a driver and a soldier when you were in the HVO. Were you aware, Mr. Tolo, Bosnian Muslim civilians were forced to dig trenches in the Vitez area while you were in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: There was a rule down there. A person who could not hold a rifle could hold a shovel or give a contribution to the state in some other way. For example, there was a work platoon consisting of the Romany. We are neighbours, and I would see them working most often, and I would see how they were organised. And it wasn't only the Romany, there were all ethnic groups in this work platoon. If they were not able to hold a rifle or if they were afraid to fight, they could hold a shovel during the night and dig and help in that way, or whatever. Everybody tried to give his own contribution to the Defence of the Lasva River Valley, regardless of ethnicity, religion, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tolo, when you said that a person who could not hold a rifle could hold a shovel or give contribution to the state in some other way, the state you're talking about is the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: I'm not talking about the state, I'm talking about the defence of the Lasva River Valley. I'm talking about Vitez, perhaps I misspoke. I'm talking about Vitez, which was surrounded then, and we were in this pot, in the very middle, and we all suffered the same destiny.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So my question to you, again, is: Were Bosnian Muslim civilians forced to dig trenches for the HVO?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: I did not see anyone who was forced to do this, in the sense of being held at gunpoint. It was natural, a work platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So when you talk about seeing the group of Romanies or gypsies digging trenches for the HVO, is it your testimony that those individuals were digging those trenches voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Not a single gypsy is going to take a shovel into his own hands and dig of his own free-will, and this is commonly known. There are many settlements of the Romany down there, and they are my neighbours, and they were organised as a work platoon, and they had a commander of their own, and they took shifts when they went out to dig. And afterwards they were returned to their villages. They received their food rations, naturally, and they were treated just like soldiers who held rifles in their hands. They got cigarettes, food and everything else that others were given, as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So given what you just said about the Romanies, that the Romanies were forced to dig trenches; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Everybody had to do his own work duty. As soon as you were of military age you had to contribute to defence in some way. If I could have not waged war I would have opted for that, but I had to work at least as a driver because that was the only way we could save our own lives, our families, and Vitez as a town in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolo, did you pick up prisoners from the cinema in downtown Vitez and take them to dig trenches in your minibus? And if so, how many times did you do it?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: I did not. I did not ever drive prisoners out to dig. I often drove civilians, but these were people mostly elderly. I didn't know what ethnicity or religion they were, because for a longer period of time I had been absent and I knew very few people because prisoners, after all, are those whose hands are tied in, who are guarded, et cetera, and I drove people who were taken up there to dig.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How many times did you drive civilians up to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Whenever necessary. I drove people who were military conscripts, because, you know, it was different. Military age men were one thing, and civilians were men who were younger than 18 or older than 65, and women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How many times did you do it, Mr. Tolo, 50, 100, 150, how many times?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Less than 50 times, I'm not too sure now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And how many civilians would you take every time you went? How many civilians would you take up to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: My minibus takes 20 persons, and again, I want to mention that these were not civilians, these were military age men.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well you told us there were elderly men in that group; didn't you?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And certainly the Bosnian Muslims weren't in the HVO; were they?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So if you took 50 trips with 20 people at a trip, that means you took approximately a thousand people to dig trenches; is that right? Would that be a rough estimate?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Most of them were the Romany from our village, and they were taken up there in groups. I don't know how many I took, really. I do not have an accurate idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were any of them shot? During your 50 trips and your thousand people, were any of those people shot when they were up there digging trenches?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Well, there were woundings, especially when the frontline would fall and then a new line would be fortified in an accelerated manner, and then some were engaged in order to keep the line until new trenches were dug. So there were woundings, yes. But there were mistakes that they made themselves. Again, I'm talking about the Romanies because I was together with them. As they were digging, when they would go to a neighbouring house, to steal a hen or whatever, something from the house, then they would cross our minefields, their minefields, and they would be wounded sometimes, when they would cross a minefield that, would happen, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So they had civilians, the people taken up there to dig trenches were both shot and wounded and also wounded by mines on the frontline; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: We had military age men who were wounded by BH army members while they were fortifying the battle positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And Mr. Tolo, when did you take these people up to dig trenches and where did you take them up to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Mostly during the night. I would take them to Bobasi, to frontlines that were held by the first battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Where? Where?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: From Kuber to -- I don't know the names in this terrain very well. To Krcevine and beyond Krcevine. Wherever necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And where did you pick these people up?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: You mean when they were on their way to do the digging?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: In their village, or, rather, in front of my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Who told you to pick them up?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Everything went through requests of certain battalions, and Mr. Vinac was responsible for the Romanies, and he would be informed that a certain group would be necessary for digging in such and such a place, and that we would have to come and report to the commander there, and that is what I did, I took them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you got your orders from Vinac; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Not my orders, but I got my orders from Mr. Zuljevic, who was head of the car-park or that part of the Vitez Brigade, regarding fuel distribution and everything else. He was in charge of that. He would give me instructions to take the vehicle to such and such a place, and it was easy for me because this was in front of my house where I would pick them up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And both Zuljevic and Vinac were in the Vitez Brigade and members of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And this taking civilians to dig trenches, people to dig trenches on the frontlines, that was an organised endeavour, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, my learned friend keeps using a term which this witness is denying repeatedly, but the Prosecutor continues to use it, hoping that the witness will forget and that it will go down into the record. The Prosecutor keeps talking about civilians. The witness says that he drove military conscripts. So I think, in the interest of correctness, proper terms should be used. Also, we are using a great deal of time, more than used for the direct-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Carry on, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolo, the people you took to dig trenches, such as the Romanies; were they members of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The Romanies were members of the HVO and they had to be forced to dig trenches; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: I have already said they were not forced, because when you use force, I understand that somebody is digging under threat of weapons. They knew that they had to do the digging, because that was their contribution. If we're talking about Romanies, they were digging trenches at Zabreza, an attack occurred, the HVO soldiers fled, throwing away their weapons. They picked up those weapons and restored control of the frontline. If they were acting under force, under coercion, why did they do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolo, prior to Mr. Nobilo's objection, did you ever call the people you took to dig trenches conscripts? Did you ever call them conscripts or did you say they were men of fighting age? How did you describe them, prior to Mr. Nobilo's objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to the form of the question. The record is clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's clear he didn't use the word "conscript" until he objected to the word.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: With all due respect to Mr. Kehoe, my friend and colleague, the witness repeatedly said that there was work obligation, there was work obligation imposed on the population. Call that conscript, call that whatever. It's clear, and it's inappropriate to question the witness about the transcript. The transcript is the transcript. He can ask him what his testimony is, but it's inappropriate to question him about the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I agree with you at least on one thing, Mr. Hayman, the transcript is the transcript, and the Judges will decide on the basis of the transcript. With respect to the merits of this question, Mr. Nobilo is the one who raised the objection as to the difference between the civilians and those who did not have the status of civilians, and Mr. Kehoe is taking that in account. He's asking the witness to describe who the civilians were, and he's trying to assess who were members of the HVO among those who were sent to dig trenches. Please don't interrupt him too often so as not to exceed the time for cross-examination. This is a very important question for the indictment, so I think it's a very legitimate question. Mr. Hayman, you have the floor one last time. You want to come back to this question?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We haven't objected as to time, Mr. President, but you've mentioned the time allotted for cross-examination. May we inquire, what is the time allotted for cross-examination? Our records reflect we're 30 minutes over the length of the direct-examination, and we have sat here patiently, with all due respect, without interrupting frequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You are very well aware of this, Mr. Hayman. This is a recurrent issue. We discussed at length among Judges on this very relevant issue. We are attempting to make sure that some kind of balance exists between cross-examination and direct-examination. We agree on this. This being said, you cannot prevent Judges, when certain questions arise, especially if the questions are important ones, you can't prevent the Judges from showing interest in what is their mission, which is to search for the truth. I agree with you, Mr. Hayman, I said this to Mr. Kehoe on several occasions. I do not want the cross-examination to be too long. Therefore, it may be better not to have too many objections put to interrupt him. Mr. Kehoe did go too far, but the question of digging trenches is a relevant one. I know this is bothering you, I can understand that, but the witness must be clear when he answers, and I think that the questions are quite accurate. But tell us, Mr. Kehoe, how long do you plan to take for the rest of your cross-examination? We know that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: About two minutes. Two minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Two minutes. Okay. Mr. Hayman, is that okay, two minutes? You seem to be happy with that. So your objection has achieved something. You'll have two minutes, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I shall add that in order to be fair we decided this: If the cross-examination is above the time for the direct-examination, we're not counting this for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But we thought that we hadn't been too far. We hadn't exceeded by too long a time. This rule is not easy to implement and it doesn't belong to my traditional proceedings. I'm trying to use it as least as I can, but never forget, Mr. Hayman, this is no civil law, this is no common-law. We are trying to carry out our mission, which is to find what the truth is, and this is the first obligation that Mr. Blaskic has towards us. He wants us to establish the truth; doesn't he? So Mr. Kehoe, you have another two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolo, how many other drivers, besides you, drove people to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: I know about myself. That is where I drove from. There was another van with a military driver, attached to the Vitez Brigade. We took turns occasionally for digging and for other tasks, but I don't know exactly. I know about myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Tolo, you know that between you and these other drivers, Bosnian Muslims were taken to the frontlines to dig trenches; weren't they?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: The ethnic affiliation of each individual is not written on his forehead. I hadn't spent much time there. I didn't know them very well. Many of my school friends got killed. I don't even know all my next door neighbours. The people were changing all the time. There were people coming in from the outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolo, are you telling these Judges that you do not know that Bosnian Muslims were taken to dig trenches by you and other drivers of the HVO? Are you telling these Judges that?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: I wish to say that if they were taken, they were taken together with others, because I wish to underline, once again, I can't tell when I see somebody in front of me that he's a Muslim or not. It doesn't say what he is on his forehead. Maybe they were, probably they were, but again, they were with others. So there was no exception as to who would go to dig. In the case of Romanies, they have a typical appearance so it's easier to tell who they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And none of these Bosnian Muslims were in the HVO; were they?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness has answered that he doesn't know whether there were any Muslims, and then the Prosecutor says, "And not one of those Muslims was in the HVO," and he has already said that he doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, you're right, Mr. Nobilo. Well, this question had already been asked by you, Mr. Kehoe. You've got one question and one minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I might have one moment, Mr. President, we may be through. Mr. President, I have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine. We're going to have a ten-minute break before resuming the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nobilo, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. Tolo, the last subject you discussed with the Prosecutor was the work obligation, so I should like to ask you a few more questions so as to assist the Court to understand what a work obligation was. You said that you refused Blaskic's offer to join the army, that is the HVO units, in the summer, in July 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In October 1992, you said that you were a driver of a minibus. Will you explain to the Court, on the basis of what were you engaged for the needs of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: There were several vans and minibuses, and everyone had to make a contribution. All this was organised through the Defence Department. We would drive once a week or twice a week, shifts to Slatkevode. We had a schedule. On the other days we would do our normal duties. I myself --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you were doing your normal duties, please explain to the Court --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me. I don't think the witness was finished. He said, "I myself," and then the question came in. With all due respect, counsel, I don't think the witness was finished responding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That is right, Mr. Nobilo. Put short questions to the witness if you want him to answer quietly, calmly. Take the time it takes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us, please, what was your private job? What were you doing on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: I was maintaining the Vitez-Travnik line for money. That was my job. As a private entrepreneur, I transported people along that line.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And for the HVO, as part of your work obligation, how many times a week or a month did you drive HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: That varied. Sometimes twice a week, sometimes once in a fortnight. So it varied.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So in this way you were performing your work obligation from the month of October in 1992 until the beginning of the war in April 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Yes, until the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Will you now tell the Court, in legal terms, is there a difference in work obligation, the kind that you performed by driving a minibus for the needs of the HVO, and the only work obligation that your neighbours, the Romanies, did by digging trenches? Is that one in the same work obligation?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: The work obligation is the same. I was making my contribution by driving and they by digging. We would have the same benefits in the sense of cigarettes and food, as far as it was possible under those circumstances, and we also got the same certificates from the HVO in terms of years of service, regulation of years of service and that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us, your work obligation in the HVO from October 1992 until April 1993, is it counted in the same way as if you were on the frontlines armed as a member of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: I, as a driver and a HVO soldier with a rifle in his hand, were treated in the same way. We had the same status.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was your work obligation recognised as part of your years of service in the same way as a soldier?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Your work obligation, is it recognised in the distribution of shares, in the transformation of socially owned enterprises into privately owned enterprises in the same way as if you were a soldier?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did the Romanies have the status of HVO soldiers in terms of years of service, pensionable years of service and shares of socialist enterprises in transition?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In the legal sense, in property terms, in terms of revenue, in terms of status, was there any difference between an HVO combatant and somebody who was participating in the war under the work obligation?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: No, everything was the same in terms of revenues, rights and every other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: As far as you know, serving in the army and work obligation, were these two components one and the same obligation?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you ever drive civilians who were under guards or under military escort going to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Where did you drive the civilians from?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Mostly from my district, Sofa, and from the downtown area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you were driving from Sofa, or from the downtown area, were the civilians rounded up by civilians, or did they come of their own accord?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: The military commanders would indicate how many people they needed and they would come and I would pick them up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did anyone ever tell you "I am a Muslim" when he went to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And were there Muslim individuals in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Yes, (redacted). He was a member of the military police. He was my school friend. He was a Muslim and a member of the HVO, and that's how I know, because we went to school together.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Let us go on to another area. You told the Prosecutor that you never saw a Blaskic order addressed to Darko Kraljevic, nor were you ever present when Blaskic and Kraljevic were having a conversation.

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: On the basis of which facts did you come to a conclusion regarding relations between Blaskic and Kordic that you told the Court about?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: As a soldier, a driver, I was in the field, surrounded by the military, among others, by the soldiers of Mr. Darko, and through their conversations they would keep saying, "You see how important Darko is? He is God and Blasko is to appeal to him." And there were other soldiers showing off in this sense, either while we were driving or while we were waiting for people to get together for us to take them wherever we were taking them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You were shown a Blaskic command on a disciplinary measure against a member of a unit Zuti on the 26th of November, 1993. So you were shown this order dated the 26th of November, 1993, punishing members of the Zuti unit. Will you explain to the Court, after Commander Tuka seriously wounded Zuti so that the latter ended up in a hospital, and after the Zuti unit killed Tuka, what happened next?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: First members of the Mujna, that is the soldiers under Tuka's command, wanted to take their revenge against members of Zuti, that is, to kill him. But they didn't manage, because after Tuka's killing, this was resolved at a different level. While Zuti was in the hospital, his personal bodyguards were with him, and the soldiers had lost their leader so they were placed under the command of another brigade, so that the number of soldiers were not the same as Zuti had before he went to the hospital. All he had left were his personal bodyguards and the others went and joined the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: While Zuti was in the hospital, which unit, and in what way was his unit subordinated?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: The only unit that was capable of such a thing, and that was the 4th Military Police Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was there an armed conflict? Were there dead?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: There was some shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: That military operation which subdued the Zuti unit and placed it under another command, did it occur before the punishment was issued or afterwards?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: It was before the measure was taken, after Tuka was killed and to prevent revenge by the Mujnas. So the military police did it before the Mujnas.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Are you trying to tell the Court that the military police first subdued the resistance of the Zuti and then disciplinary measures were taken?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Yes, I tried to say before that Mr. Blaskic would occasionally try to create conditions to establish his control. At the beginning that was not possible, but as time passed he gained more control over individual units and manifested his authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Let us go to another area, very quickly, now. The Prosecutor showed you the orders that Blaskic issued for starting training as far back as 1992. Tell the Court, did you ever hear of, before the months of August and September, when the training centre in New Bila started working, where you worked too, did anybody ever organise that before?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: In the area of the Lasva River Valley I never heard of training facilities nor did I ever see one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You told me during the break that the screen was not very clear to you. Could you please look at the photograph showing the soldiers, if possible, just look at the photograph from over here.

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: (Complies)

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Please sit down. Did you perhaps recognise any of these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Yes, I did. The second one behind, the one at the second row, rather, they are actually the young soldiers who had completed training at our course, and they ended up in the military police. I don't know the other men by their names, because I really worked with all of them and for a very short period of time. I know them because I would meet them afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Are you trying to tell us that that is precisely these young soldiers that you had trained?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Now let us move on to a new area. The Prosecutor tried to get an answer from you which would say that the territorial principle that was taken over from the JNA and the principle one village, one unit are the same. Now I'm asking you the following: In the Territorial Defence, where were weapons and equipment, and who distributed it?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: It was in warehouses, and equipment was distributed at the command post where people would come after they received papers to come. So they would get everything from the warehouse, food, ammunition, and weapons, et cetera, that is to say, according to the Territorial Defence principle of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And what about the village, how did the village get equipment and food? I mean in the HVO organisation.

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: They bought it mostly on their own. They would procure it in different ways. They would steal it. They would inherit it. And these same weapons were on them all the time, and they kept it at home as their own property, not as part of the military inventory, but as their own things.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In the territorial principle of the JNA, who appointed the entire command structure?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: The general staff, and there was a commander who said who would be in charge of what. There was a structure. So it's not from the village that somebody was issuing orders, but the main staff that commanded a broader area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And in the HVO village unit principle, who appointed the commanders there?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: The locals on their own. They chose their commander, and usually this would be a strong guy, somebody who they would be afraid of, perhaps, who would not really meet their requirements, but who would try to fulfill their interests to the greatest possible degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that in the HVO one village was one unit. What was the name of Territorial Defence units and how were they set up?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: After doing one's military service, one had a military booklet saying exactly where one's post was. And in case papers were sent, then people would have to respond and to come for an exercise, and then a unit would be set up, up to the level of company or battalion. But in this other situation, the entire village was a unit. So it could have been a group of 40 people or a group of 100 people, and they would all be called that village's company.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And the Territorial Defence had detachments; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: That's correct, several villages, because it depended on the size of the village how many villages would be part of one detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And my last area of questioning. You confirmed to the Prosecutor that Blaskic had a strong personality, that he was a psychologist, that he was knowledgeable, that he knew the rules of discipline and he knew how to wield authority. We are saying all of this in terms of the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And now I'm asking you the following: These characteristics of his, this knowledge of his, the knowledge that you also acquired in the JNA academy, was it usable at all in Vitez in the situation that you were in at that time, and with the army, the troops that Blaskic had under his command?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: With that mode of work, no, and with the knowledge he had, no, no, he had to change. He had to adjust to the new environment, but not with ones like that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And in your opinion, was Blaskic more able, more skillful in the situation that he had in the JNA or the situation that he found in Vitez? Where did he feel better, and where was he more efficient and effective?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: In the former JNA, naturally, that is where he could show his right results. I mean, his true value, that is what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: That would be all, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Nobilo. I am now turning to my fellow Judges. Judge Riad you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good afternoon, Mr. Tolo. I would like to follow on from the last questions put by Mr. Nobilo. You said that the then Colonel and then General Blaskic was an exemplary commander in all respects. This may imply that he was respected and obeyed by his soldiers. Or was his authority challenged, violated? What do you think?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: In the former army, that is to say, in the JNA, all the soldiers respected him and they could not disobey his orders. He was an exemplary officer in the former JNA. He came to Vitez as a stranger, a person from the outside, imposed upon someone to the local commanders, and the local commanders were not pleased to see someone else take over something that they had created, the way they had created it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Did you notice cases of open challenges to his authority?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Well, the first case of this kind for me was the bad stories that were being told among the rank and file. They did not trust General Blaskic, and that is the first way they opposed his authority and his knowledge, that is to say, while I was in Vitez among the rank and file soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I believe this is often the case, rank and file soldiers often criticise their officers. But would they show openly that they didn't follow his orders? Apart from the fact they were criticising him, would they show open rebellion? Would they openly not obey his orders?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: I don't know whether General Blaskic ever directly gave orders to such a soldier, all of this went through other commanders, too. And now these higher echelons, how much they limited his scope of authority or not, that I don't know. I mean, I'm not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Well, this forces me to ask you another question and get some specific data as to your rank in the HVO. There seems to be some contradiction between the summary that was given of your testimony and your testimony as such. In the summary I quote, "He declined to join the HVO military and instead undertook various alternative forms of service." You were in the HVO. You did not refuse to join the HVO. You were in it, weren't you? So you are in it or you're out of it.

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Your Honour, at that time, General Blaskic asked me to take part in combat, as an active officer in the Lasva River Valley, in the HVO. However, at that time I had been wounded, physically, so I was physically incapable of carrying out this duty, and for various other reasons that I mentioned. But later, as I started this private activity of my own, in terms of transportation, I was automatically subjected to this work obligation within the scope of defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: As an HVO officer, or as a civilian?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: As a soldier/driver at that time. In my documents perhaps they mentioned my rank from the former JNA, but I was a soldier/driver, in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I believe that you took part in training the younger people. There was a training programme coming from Vukovic, and did you carry out the training?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: From October 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I see. And this training programme was aimed at training soldiers; was it a serious one, or not? And this was a programme that existed before you, or was it not?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: I don't know what curriculum they had before I came up there, but according to the knowledge and skills that the soldiers had exhibited, the trainees had exhibited, I suggested to Mr. Vukovic that we work according to my own training programme. So the point was to actually teach the soldiers what I had been teaching them. So I was the one who wrote my own plan and programme.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Before that, there was training, this was part of a continuous training; wasn't it? You were not the first one to train HVO troops.

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: That was the first group of soldiers who were trained in that training centre. Before that were the people who came before me. These same trainees had been in the same barracks a month or two before I arrived. So I came there as an instructor among junior soldiers. But this was the first group and the last one that was in these barracks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And were they properly trained? Were they well trained, or not?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: No way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You testified -- I wrote down your words. You said that each unit was independent and would not encroach on another unit's territory or tasks. Still, all these units were under the same command; weren't they? As is the case in administration, you have several departments or services, but they are all under one and the same command. So in the military, in the same way, they were under the same command and would obey the same commanding officer; wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I don't understand what period you're asking me about. Because during the initial period they did have the same task, and they were all fighting to defend the Lasva River Valley. But specifically, the special purposes units did not have their own joint commander in the Lasva River Valley in the initial period. But afterwards, when they were encircled as the war continued, if somebody was above Darko, there was no one who was in contact with him. And they were aware, themselves, they had to put one another under somebody's command in order to get ammunition, food, et cetera, so they needed it for logistics purposes. But they really had to see what their own estimates were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So everybody was waging war the way they pleased?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: How should I put it, there were several gangs or troops, so this would come down to guerrilla?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Well, on the one hand you could describe it that way, but with the same objective, the same ultimate objective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: There is something else I would like to know. I would like to have some details as to the trenches that were being dug at the time. You are in an excellent position to know who is a Muslim and who is a Croat, given that you have parents in both ethnic groups. If you would transport people to places where they were supposed to dig trenches, you were not in a position to ascertain from the way they would speak, their accents, whether they were Croats or Muslim?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: I left when I was 17 years old. I went to military schools. I talked to everyone. My official language was the Serbian version with Ejekavica (phoen). Because when I came back to Vitez, I had a lot of problems, because I spoke the Ejekavica, the Serbian version, and when somebody looked at me they would have thought I was a Serb, judging by my accent. So first of all, I had to get used to speaking the Ejekavica again, our language. And how could I possibly discern what other people were? I simply couldn't tell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But were there Muslims, or not, by their names?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: I don't know these people. I just arrived there in 1992, and I didn't manage to get to know these people. Had somebody introduced themselves to me, then I could have said more or less who this person was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You said that no matter who they were, whether they were Romanies, Croats or Serbs, these people were willingly going to dig trenches. Did anybody among them try to flee? And what would happen if somebody was trying to flee?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: As far as the Romanies are concerned, there were some cases when they would escape from trench digging, but then others would cover up for him. So that's the way they handled things, but nobody went to dig voluntarily. I mean, me, for one, I would not like to be engaged in this military work obligation. I would prefer to make a hundred Deutschemarks doing other things, but then I knew that the military police would be after me and I would have to pay a fine and disciplinary action would be taken against me. But since the Romanies were all from one village, they managed to cover up these individual cases when people would escape to their homes. So the commanders did not realise what had happened, so they couldn't take any action against them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes, but they were being guarded when they would dig trenches. They were under the supervision of soldiers who were making sure they wouldn't escape, or was that just to work, what they were doing?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: I already mentioned once, there weren't any military escorts or guards. They were simply brought up there to the frontline where the soldiers were in front of them. The soldiers were out there in the field or behind a rock or whatever, and then they were supposed to dig the trenches where these soldiers were supposed to go into. And, of course, they normally talked to these soldiers, and there were breaks, naturally, and during the break there was no problem to leave, because they usually worked at night, anyway. They, of course, did not have to go in front of the rifles, but they were running back home to the back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So you would take people, or what you call the civilians or the military, you would take them to places that were very close to the frontline; is that so? Very close to the enemy, actually.

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: That was the frontline, naturally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So they could be hit by the enemy? The enemy could shoot at them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: The characteristic of the terrain was that we could be hit when we were in the centre of town, because they were everywhere and they were so near BiH. For example, sometimes the frontlines were 500 metres away, as the crow flies, so all of it was the frontline.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: One last question: You said that criminals were being recruited for the Vitezovi; who would recruit those criminals?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: They volunteered. It's not that anybody had to recruit them and that any one of them would show up and say "I'm a criminal." They would say that they want to volunteer, to be part of the PPN, the special purposes units and the HVO. Darko Kraljevic was in charge of this, together with his commanders, and nobody put any questions to them, and nobody asked them for any documents, and they didn't have to give police records or anything to show whether they were criminals or not. But afterwards they would take advantage of this, in terms of the crimes that they wanted to commit anyway. They didn't do it all the time, but they would go out and commit robbery, for example. But everybody was afraid of Darko, so nobody dared initiate proceedings against these people, so they actually got asylum within the Vitezovi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But was there no way of sorting through these recruits? It would be dangerous for any army to take anybody in. Were they not trying to see what were the incidents of these would-be soldiers? That might have proved dangerous for the army, couldn't it?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: As far as I know there wasn't a special selection involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tolo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you Judge Riad. I give the floor to Judge Shahabuddeen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Tolo, I'm trying to grasp the meaning of what you said concerning these independent units. Would the position have corresponded to the popular idea of a warlord? You know, a warlord is supposed to be a military commander who has supreme and unquestioned authority in his own area. He may have understandings or agreements with other warlords, but in his own area his authority is supreme. Was that the idea that you were putting forward?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: As General -- or, rather, Colonel Blaskic came. That was probably what happened, because they brought in a person who had very good prospects in that other army, so he could only be helpful and he could only contribute to the creation of this army. So the idea was certainly there. After all at the end of the war he did carry this through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Am I correct in understanding you this way: There was an evolution in the system, and that gradually there appeared a more structured form of military authority with one supreme commander at the top? Is that the idea, that there was this gradual evolution?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Yes. Gradually a central authority was being established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Could you help me with this last point? At what point of time would you say that the evolution had reached a point where General Blaskic was able to exercise effective authority throughout the military structure?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: For me, from my own point of view, when he activated me and when he replaced these untrained and uneducated officers who were only there by virtue of their physical strength, and when he appointed officers from the reserve corps, and also when he would break-up the PPNs, the Special Purposes Units now and then, it is perhaps that period, September or October 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tolo. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: You're welcome, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Tolo, I only have a couple of questions for you because my colleagues have put all the questions I had in mind to ask, and I thank them for it. You were in charge of training; weren't you? Is that so?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: Yes, from October onwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: And during the training of those soldiers, who happened to be soldiers, sort of makeshift soldiers who were actually villagers, given the hierarchy you were under, did you think of trying to make them aware of the Laws and Customs of War, of telling them, "This can be done but this may not be done," or did you not try at all?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: There were several instructors, and specifically I was in charge of teaching them how to handle weapons, how to use weapons. So there were several instructors and each one of them had his own area of instruction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: And were there instructors in charge of teaching the laws of war?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: I would call this theory, classical theory, and that was carried out by commanders of platoons and squads. So what was less important at that time -- in those times, that is what they did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, but let's be clear. There is a trend to tell us that commanders would not have such authority, and we heard and we often had the impression that the training was not carried out. Maybe regrettably so. So this is a very simple question I'm putting to you. You are telling me that this activity was not within the scope of your activities. I'm asking you now whether in that same training centre there were colleagues of yours who were in charge of providing this theory. You can answer in a very simple way, by yes or no.

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: In the teaching centre, theory was taught by commanders of platoons and commanders of squads, et cetera, and I was there only for a professional training and for subject matter that they were not sufficiently familiar with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But when you would discuss with colleagues coming from the other training fields, would they tell you, "Yesterday I'm going to tell them what they may do with civilians, what they may not do with them." Would such cases take place or were you left in the dark altogether?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: The instructors who were with me were for tactical operations, for engineering, and that part would belong to Mr. Zvonko Vukovic, and I was not familiar with the teaching plan and programme that he had made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine. I shall not insist on this. I believe you are a driver, or you were a driver for the HVO, but you had some prior military training; is that right? Hence, a very simple question I'd like to put to you. Why did Colonel Blaskic not use you for higher positions or jobs, regardless of your wounding?

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: You mean after arriving in Vitez, after Tuzla? After I arrived in Vitez, you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: EDVARD TOLO
utterances.text: First of all, it was my wish to take a short break, and basically to stay away from military operations and from the military in general from any point of view. He did not tell me then that I would be an instructor, whatever, but he simply mentioned rank to me, and rank would be followed by assignments that he would give me later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine. Mr. Tolo, I have no further questions for you. I think you can be released. Thank you very much for coming to the Tribunal to testify before it, for trying to answer the best you could all the questions that you heard. Do not move. It's nearly five past six or 6.00. I think this clock has not been adjusted yet. The only one not to have been adjusted by the Tribunal yet. So we have the feeling we worked even harder than we did. Anyway, the hearing is adjourned. We shall resume tomorrow at 10.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
